<a id="s1"></a>
## 1. Intro
- Design Dropbox, also called design Google Drive; largely the same question
- Asked at all top FAANGs
  - Really popular at Google and Amazon; shows up a ton at Meta too
- Evan has asked it "maybe around 50 times" at Meta and Hello Interview
- On the easier side
  - Asked most often of mid-level (E4 / L4)
  - Also shows up a ton for senior and staff
- He calls out level deltas as he goes
- Written version on hellointerview.com; vote page for the next question

<a id="s2"></a>
## 2. Roadmap
- For any user-facing product design
  1. Requirements: functional (core features) + non-functional (qualities)
  2. Core entities: persisted and exchanged via the APIs
  3. API: user-facing endpoints
  4. High-level design: boxes and arrows; primary goal = satisfy the functional requirements
     - Relatively simple at this point
  5. Deep dives: expand so the system scales, is fault tolerant, meets the NFRs

<a id="s3"></a>
## 3. Functional requirements
- Identify the top three features
  - System you know: easy; otherwise ask the interviewer
- Requirements
  1. Upload a file to remote storage
  2. Download a file from remote storage
  3. Automatically sync files across devices
     - A local folder on your desktop
     - A file uploaded to remote is synced to the local file system
     - A file dropped into the local folder is uploaded to remote, then synced to all other connected devices
- Out of scope: rolling our own blob storage
  - That's a different question (design S3)

<a id="s4"></a>
## 4. Non-functional requirements
- Qualities: low latency, fault tolerance, durability, CAP…
- Most candidates breeze through with generic words; "entirely uninformative"
- For senior / staff+, NFRs inform the deep dives; depth is needed for those levels
- CAP
  - Partition tolerance is a must at this scale
  - **Availability >> consistency**
  - In context: someone in Germany changes a file; someone in America reads the old version shortly after
    - That's fine; we accept it so everyone can always download / view
- **Low latency upload and download**
  - Not the buzzword; in the context of uploads and downloads
  - Quantify? Files vary, so "a cop out": as low as possible
- **Support large files, as large as 50 GB**
  - "This is actually exactly what Dropbox supports"
  - **Resumable uploads**
    - A 50 GB upload takes time; losing internet halfway shouldn't mean starting over
- **High data integrity (sync accuracy)**
  - Eventual consistency is fine (a couple of seconds)
  - Once stabilized, local folder, remote, and other folders match
- Fine to come back and add NFRs as you go

<a id="s5"></a>
## 5. On estimation
- Not done up front, on purpose; his general suggestion
- Know the scale: Dropbox has hundreds of millions of DAU
- Storage: nearly infinitely scalable blob storage (S3 or other cloud blob storage), so it doesn't matter much
- Estimations are important; do them in the HLD when the result directly impacts the design
  - Up-front DAU / storage / bandwidth math, then "wow, that's a ton": a waste of time
  - The interviewer only learns you can multiply and divide
- Overcommunicate: tell the interviewer that's your approach; he expects they won't disagree

<a id="s6"></a>
## 6. Core entities
- He says "core entities", not data model / schema, intentionally
  - Five minutes in, you don't know all the columns yet
- **File**: the raw bytes; stored in S3 or other blob storage
- **File metadata**: file name, ID, MIME type, size, …
- **User**: least important; maybe even a distraction
- Columns: you can list them inline; he documents them next to the database during the HLD

<a id="s7"></a>
## 7. API (first guess)
- Entities are the inputs and outputs; at least one endpoint per FR

```text
POST /files -> 200
body: File, FileMetadata

GET /files/:fileId -> File & FileMetadata

GET /changes?since={timestamp} -> fileId[]
```

- Sync: clients ask "what changed?", then call upload / download
- Shorthand referencing entities lets you move faster; many candidates spend too long here
- One-to-one mapping with FRs here; not always the case
- "Astute viewers" will notice these are wrong
  - Upload is not a single `POST /files`
  - Most candidates don't know that at this point; that's okay
  - Run with the first guess; amend after the deep dives
- No user ID in the body
  - Comes from the header via session token or JWT
  - Otherwise anyone could upload / download on behalf of another user
  - Minor; most interviewers won't care, some will

<a id="s8"></a>
## 8. HLD: upload and download
- Go one by one through the APIs (they satisfy the FRs)
- **Load balancer + API gateway** (could be AWS managed API Gateway)
  - Middleware: authentication, rate limiting, SSL termination
  - Routing to the correct microservice
- **File service**
- Upload (simple version)
  1. Client sends file + metadata to the file service
  2. File service uploads the bytes to **blob storage (S3)**
     - Raw bytes go to blob storage "almost every single time": cheap for large blobs
     - GCP etc. also fine
  3. S3 returns a link to the file
  4. File service writes the **file metadata DB**
  5. Return 200 (or an error code)
- Two different stores because the data is very different in nature
- File metadata (written next to the DB, so it can evolve)
  - fileId, fileName, mimeType (PDF, image…), size (bytes)
  - ownerId (FK to user), potentially shared (out of scope)
  - S3 link
  - Other less important metadata
- Download
  1. `GET` with fileId hits the file service
  2. Look up metadata; it holds the S3 link
  3. Return metadata; client downloads directly from S3
     - Not download to the file service, then again to the client
- Upload / download work now, "granted small files"; optimizations in the deep dives

<a id="s9"></a>
## 9. HLD: sync
- Usually the client box is small and abstract
  - Not here: Dropbox (and streaming / adaptive bitrate: Spotify, Netflix, YouTube) has important client logic
- Client contains
  - **Local folder**: the synced folder
  - **Client app**: downloaded on Mac / iPhone / Windows; syncs remote and local folder
- Two sync directions
  1. Remote changed: poll for changes periodically, download the new file, replace the old
  2. Local changed: upload changed files to remote
- Remote changed
  - New **sync service**
    - Arguably over-modularizing vs. the file service; it will grow in the deep dives
  - `getChanges` asks the file service to query metadata for changed IDs
    - Needs `createdAt` and `updatedAt` on file metadata
  - Client then fetches metadata per ID and downloads from S3
  - Extra round trip noticed: make `getChanges` return full metadata instead of IDs
- Local changed
  - OS APIs watch a folder for changes
    - Windows: `FileSystemWatcher`
    - macOS: `FSEvents`
  - On change: upload via the normal path; re-upload to S3, change S3 link, update `updatedAt`
- How do we know we already have a file locally?
  - **Local DB** on the client: metadata incl. IDs for each local file
  - Map fileId to its location in the local folder
  - Cross-reference local metadata with remote; keep them as consistent as possible
  - **Fingerprinting** to hash and identify files: saved for the deep dives
- HLD meets all FRs

<a id="s10"></a>
## 10. Deep dives: level expectations
- Goal: satisfy the NFRs
- Mid-level: this board is "close to getting hired"; interviewer asks follow-ups
- Senior / staff: keep driving; go one by one through NFRs
  - Senior: deep in one to two places
  - Staff: deep in two to three places
  - More hands-on experience, more depth
- He goes into more areas than an interview needs, to teach

<a id="s11"></a>
## 11. Deep dive: large files (50 GB) + resumable uploads
- Out of order, because it affects other NFRs
- He'd tell even a mid-level candidate: this only works for 5–10 MB files
- Issue 1: redundant upload path
  - Upload once to the file service, again to blob storage
  - Wastes bandwidth and server CPU
- Issue 2: request body limits
  - Set by browsers, servers, API gateways
  - AWS managed API Gateway: 10 MB POST body
  - A 50 GB file gets an error
- Fix issue 1: **upload directly to S3 via a pre-signed URL**
  1. Send only metadata to the file service
  2. File service writes metadata, e.g. `status: started`
  3. File service requests a pre-signed URL from blob storage
     - "I'm authenticated; I want to upload a PDF of this size"
     - S3 returns a secure link with signed metadata: only that MIME type, only that size, only for a limited time
     - Doesn't remember S3's default; "let's say 10, 15, 30 minutes"
  4. Return the URL to the client
  5. Client uploads directly to S3 with the pre-signed URL (not our API)
- Remaining issue: time and failure
  - 50 GB at 100 Mbps average internet = **1 hour 12 minutes** (math done before filming)
  - Losing the connection halfway and restarting "would suck"
- **Chunking**
  - Chunk files on the client into ~5 MB chunks
  - Upload chunks to S3 serially or in parallel, depending on bandwidth
  - Track which chunks are uploaded; on failure, upload only the missing ones
- Database choice aside
  - Any common SQL or NoSQL works
  - SQL vs NoSQL debate "kind of outdated"; well configured they do largely the same things
  - SQL (Postgres): normalize; a chunks table with FK to metadata
  - He picks **DynamoDB**: chunks as a list on the metadata object
    - Each chunk: id, status, S3 link
- Flow
  1. Chunk the 50 GB file; send metadata with all chunks, status "not started"
  2. Upload chunks; update status to uploaded and the S3 link
  3. Resume: fetch metadata, compare client chunks to stored chunks, upload missing ones
- **Fingerprinting**
  - Need a unique way to say "this chunk equals that uploaded chunk"
  - Maintaining indexes: "silly", error-prone
  - Fingerprint = hash of the chunk's bytes; used as the chunk ID
  - Compare client fingerprints with stored fingerprints; re-upload missing ones
- Updating chunk status (the hand-waved part)
  - Obvious way is insecure: client uploads, then PATCHes "complete"
    - Client could lie; metadata inconsistent with S3
    - "Hackers could only mess up their own upload" argument, but inconsistency causes debugging headaches
  - **Trust but verify**
    - Client reports "chunk uploaded" to the file service
    - File service checks with blob storage, then updates status
  - Alternative: blob-storage change notifications (**S3 notifications**)
    - S3 notifies the file service on each new chunk; client not trusted at all
    - Works; added complexity; trade-offs
  - **S3 multipart upload** exposes this chunk / upload / validate flow as an API
    - With multipart upload, S3 doesn't send a notification per part: "nuance there"
    - "If you didn't use multipart upload, you'd probably want to use multipart upload"
  - He'd go with trust but verify in an interview; both options great

<a id="s12"></a>
## 12. Deep dive: low-latency upload and download
- Chunking already helps
  - Bandwidth is fixed; chunking makes the most of it
  - Parallel chunks, adaptive chunk sizes by network condition
- **CDN**
  - Candidates like to add one; it brings content closer to users
  - Top candidates weigh whether it's needed
  - Strong argument it's not: users mostly download their own files, likely near the data center
    - Imagine the system replicated in maybe five data centers
  - Helps only for travelers or super popular shared files (e.g. Declaration of Independence)
  - CDNs are expensive; no right or wrong; he opts out
- **Compression** to transfer fewer bytes (e.g. gzip)
  - Cost: decompression on the other side
  - Text, DOCX compress well
  - JPEG, PNG, MP4 already compressed: only a couple percent gain; not worth it
  - Intelligent compression on the client by file type and network condition
  - Add `compressionAlgo` to file metadata

<a id="s13"></a>
## 13. Deep dive: sync (fast + consistent)
- Two goals: sync fast (within reason), sync consistent (local == remote)
- Fast: detecting changes
  - Periodic polling: "I think this is still the best approach"
  - **Adaptive polling**: shorter interval when the app is open or many recent changes
  - WebSockets: "totally overkill"
    - Always-on persistent connection while the computer is on; needs a WebSocket manager
    - Product question: milliseconds vs tens of seconds or a minute?
    - A refresh button can kick off a poll
  - Long polling: doesn't fit; for expected responses within ~a minute; we don't know when changes come
- Fast: **delta sync** (what he thinks Dropbox calls it)
  - Only fetch changed chunks; add `updatedAt` per chunk
  - New file: download everything, update local DB
  - Changed file: download only chunks updated since the last poll; client stitches
- Consistent: what polling means
  - Option 1: poll the DB directly
    - Add `folderId` to metadata
    - "For folder 123, give me files with chunks changed since last sync"
  - Option 2: **event bus with a cursor** (closer to what Dropbox does)
    - E.g. Kafka; every change goes on the bus
    - Folder entity with a **sync cursor**
    - First setup: replay all events to build local state; save cursor
    - Next poll: read events after the cursor; apply to local DB
    - Partition by user ID or folder ID; snapshots to avoid replaying everything
    - Great for audit trail, version control, data recovery, roll back / forward
    - Not in our requirements: "overkill"; adds a ton of complexity
    - Overwriting chunks in the DB loses old versions; the event bus could keep them
  - He deletes it from the design; opts for simplicity (poll the DB)
- **Reconciliation**
  - Local and remote can still drift (bugs, connection issues)
  - Periodically (daily / weekly) the client fetches remote state for the folder
  - Compares with local DB and fingerprints of local files; fixes issues

<a id="s14"></a>
## 14. Corrected API
- Upload doesn't post the file body; it goes directly to S3

```text
POST /files -> presignedUrl
body: FileMetadata

PUT {presignedUrl}
body: FileChunk

PATCH /files -> 200
body: Partial<FileMetadata>   // chunk status updates

GET /files/:fileId -> File & FileMetadata

GET /changes?since={timestamp} -> FileMetadata[]
```

<a id="s15"></a>
## 15. Wrap-up
- All five steps done; "a pretty good system that balances simplicity with meeting all requirements"
- New video every ~3 weeks; vote page; invites corrections in comments
  - Done in "one-ish take", not well rehearsed; may have misspoken

<a id="s16"></a>
## 16. Board

![Excalidraw board from the video](data:image/png;base64,)

- Text version, assembled from the talk

```text
 Client [Client App | Local DB | Local Folder]
   |  (download directly from S3; upload directly to S3 with pre-signed URL) --> Blob Storage (S3)
   v                                                                              ^ request pre-signed URL
 LB & API Gateway (auth, rate limiting, SSL termination, routing)                 |
   |-- upload(file, fileMetadata), getFile(fileId) --> File Service --write--> File Metadata (DynamoDB)
   |-- getChanges() -----------------------------> Sync Service <--> File Service
```

- File metadata: fileId, folderId, fileName, mimeType, size, compressionAlgo, ownerId, s3Link, createdAt, updatedAt, status 'started', chunks [{ id = fingerprint, status, s3Link, updatedAt }]
- Folder: cursor (sync cursor)
- Large files: 50 GB @ 100 Mbps = 1 hr 12 min
  1. Chunk files on client into 5 MB chunks
  2. Fingerprint each chunk: hash(bytes)
  3. Upload directly to S3
  4. Update chunk metadata with completed status
